name: Anagain
lead: Anagain (also written AnaGain) is a cosmetic hair-care ingredient derived from the sprouts of the pea plant, marketed in topical hair-growth serums and lotions and, in an oral form branded AnaGain Nu, in supplements. It is a branded cosmetic active rather than a drug, and it is used by people who want thicker-looking, fuller hair or less shedding; it is discussed in appearance communities alongside other hair-growth actives such as Redensyl, Procapil, Capixyl and Baicapil [1].

Published human evidence is limited to small, short studies. A short communication in Phytotherapy Research reported that a fluid containing 2% pea sprout extract applied to a defined scalp zone in 10 volunteers raised expression of the hair-relevant genes FGF7 and noggin by 56 and 85 percent; the same paper described a pilot supplement study in 21 volunteers in which 100 mg a day for 8 weeks reduced hair loss from day 28 onward [2]. A 2025 review of cosmeceutical hair-loss actives lists AnaGain among the ingredients it examines and notes that such products are heavily promoted on social media [1].
Laboratory work in human dermal papilla cells and mice has proposed that pea sprout extract activates Wnt/beta-catenin signaling and has antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [5].

paras: Anagain is the trade name of a pea sprout extract used as an active in hair serums, lotions and some supplements. Cosmetic reviews group it with other branded peptide and plant actives that are formulated into serums, oils and shampoos and marketed for hair growth [1]. In practice it often appears as one ingredient in a multi-ingredient serum; one commercial serum evaluated in a 2025 open-label study listed Redensyl, rice water extract, chia seed extract, rosemary oil, MelanoGray and AnaGain together [4].

In the volunteer study of a 2% pea sprout extract fluid, expression of fibroblast growth factor-7 (FGF7) and noggin in the treated scalp zone was raised by 56 and 85 percent; both are genes relevant to hair follicle biology [2].

A 2025 laboratory and mouse study reported that pea sprout extract promoted hair follicle regeneration and prolonged the anagen phase, activated Wnt/beta-catenin signaling in human dermal papilla cells, raised IGF-1 and FGF7, lowered IL-1 beta and BMP4, and showed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity that may protect follicles [5]. These are preclinical findings.

The Phytotherapy Research short communication described two parts. In the first, 10 volunteers applied a 2% pea sprout extract fluid to a defined scalp area and gene expression was measured. In the second, a pilot nutrition study in 21 volunteers gave 100 mg a day of pea sprout extract (AnaGain Nu) for 8 weeks and reported significantly reduced hair loss starting at 28 days (p < 0.002) with no adverse events [2]. The authors state in their introduction that pea sprout extract has previously been reported to improve hair density when applied topically [2]. A later paper refers to this as a randomized clinical trial in which 100 mg daily for 8 weeks significantly increased hair density [5].

No large randomized controlled trial of Anagain against placebo or minoxidil was found. A 2025 review of hype-driven topical actives says such ingredients have mostly been studied in combined formulations with other agents, with limited sample sizes, few comparisons with standard therapies, nondisclosure of the type of alopecia treated and conflicts of interest, and suggests they may serve as add-on therapy or as alternatives for patients not suited to conventional drugs [1].

Other cosmetic serum studies involve multi-ingredient products. In a 32-person study of a serum applied daily for 60 days, hair growth rate rose by 10.52 percent at 30 days and 31.62 percent at 60 days with no adverse events reported [3]. An open-label single-arm study of the Soulflower Rosemary Redensyl serum, which includes AnaGain, in healthy women measured hair growth, density, anagen:telogen ratio and graying by phototrichogram [4]. Because these serums contain several actives, the contribution of pea sprout extract cannot be separated.

The ingredient appears in forum discussion mainly as one of several alternatives or add-ons to finasteride and minoxidil. A 2025 trichology review describes the cosmeceutical hair-serum market as flooded with such actives and says it is driven by social-media marketing, while summarising the clinical evidence available for each ingredient [1]. Brands often combine it with Redensyl, rosemary oil and peptides, so users commonly encounter it inside a blend rather than alone [4].

No adverse events were reported in the oral pilot study, the volunteer gene-expression study or the cited serum studies [2][3]. These studies were small and short, and no long-term safety data were found.

card.summary: Pea-sprout extract sold in cosmetic hair serums; backed by one tiny 10-person gene-expression study.
card.note: Evidence limited to a very small, short study of gene expression.

quick.overview:
Anagain is a branded extract from pea sprouts used in over-the-counter hair serums. It is promoted as a topical hair-growth active.
Published evidence consists of a small study of 10 volunteers measuring gene expression after applying a 2% extract, and a review that lists it among hyped cosmeceutical actives.
quick.mechanism: Manufacturers and the one small study describe an effect on expression of genes involved in hair growth; this has not been shown to translate into measured hair-count outcomes in large trials.
quick.risks: No safety problems have been identified, but no large safety data exist. It is a cosmetic ingredient, not an approved hair-loss drug.

chain: Pea sprout extract applied to the scalp or taken as a supplement
Proposed shift in growth-factor signaling in the follicle
angle.text: People apply serums containing Anagain, or take the oral extract, aiming for less shedding and thicker-looking hair. The ingredient has been tested in small studies measuring gene expression and shedding, and it is often used as one ingredient among several in a serum.
